title: Speculation and deduction
tagline: Reading the evidence and choosing how sure you sound: must, might, could or can't.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (must / can't / have)
Listening Part 3 — inferring what speakers mean from clues
why: You don't always know the facts — sometimes you only have evidence, and you have to guess how certain you are. B2 First expects you to judge that certainty precisely: must is not the same as might, and getting the modal wrong changes the whole meaning of the sentence, in the present and in the past.

diagrams.title: How sure does the speaker sound?

rows.label: Certain, positive
cells: Liam must have missed the bus.

rows.label: Possible
cells: They might be stuck in traffic.
They might have changed the plan.

head: Modal
Certainty
Present example
Past example
rows: She must be tired after the match.
She must have trained really hard.
He can't have read the whole book already.
They couldn't have known about the change.

use.point: Deduction about the present, from something you can see or hear now

examples.text: The lights are off, so Miss Vega must be out of the classroom.
That can't be Liam's phone ringing — his is still on the desk.
Sofia isn't answering her messages, so she might be asleep already.

use.point: Deduction about the past, from evidence you find later

examples.text: The pitch is completely wet, so it must have rained all night.
examples.note: must have + participle = certain about a finished past event

examples.text: Nadia looks exhausted; she can't have slept more than a few hours.
examples.note: can't have = impossible, based on how she looks now

examples.text: Someone could have left the window open, but we're not sure who.
examples.note: could have = a possible explanation, not the only one

use.point: An action that was probably or certainly happening at a specific moment

examples.text: Mateo didn't hear his name; he must have been listening to music.
examples.note: continuous form for an action in progress

examples.text: They might have been waiting outside when the doors finally opened.

use.point: Everyday guesses about people, plans and results

examples.text: The results should be on the noticeboard by lunchtime, if nothing has changed.
examples.note: should = expected, based on a plan

examples.text: You can't have finished the whole essay already — you only started an hour ago.

watch_out.wrong: She must to be at home now.
watch_out.why: No to after a modal verb — the bare infinitive follows directly.

watch_out.wrong: He mustn't be at school; his bag is here.
watch_out.right: He can't be at school; his bag is here.
watch_out.why: Mustn't means it is forbidden, not it is impossible. Use can't for a negative deduction.

watch_out.wrong: They must have leave without us.
watch_out.why: The past participle follows have, not the infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: She might have been arrive late because of the traffic.
watch_out.right: She might have arrived late because of the traffic.
watch_out.why: Use the past participle after have, not the base form or the continuous form of a state that already finished.

watch_out.wrong: It's raining, so the match could be cancel.
watch_out.right: It's raining, so the match could be cancelled.
watch_out.why: When the subject receives the action, the modal needs the passive: could be + past participle.

dialogue.title: Where's Mateo?
dialogue.context: Sofia, Liam and Nadia are waiting for Mateo outside the science lab before an exam review session in Lima.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: He's ten minutes late. He must have overslept — he was coding until midnight.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Or he might have missed the bus. He usually catches the 7.40.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: His phone is off. That can't be a good sign — he never turns it off.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Wait, isn't that his bike outside the gate? He must be in the building already.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: You're right. He could be in the library finishing the reading.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Or he might have gone straight to see Miss Vega about the deadline.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That makes sense. He must have been worrying about that essay all weekend.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Look, there he is. He can't have heard us calling — he's got headphones on.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Sorry — I must have set my alarm for the wrong time.

items.sentence: The classroom is empty and the lights are off. Everyone ___ gone home already.
items.why: evidence about a finished past situation → must have + participle

items.sentence: That ___ be Nadia at the door — she's on a school trip until Friday.
items.why: impossible, because of what we know → can't

items.sentence: I'm not sure where Liam is, but he ___ be in the music room; he often practises there.
The pitch is completely dry, so it ___ rained last night.
items.why: dry pitch = impossible that it rained → can't have

items.sentence: They booked the tickets weeks ago, so the seats ___ be confirmed by now.
items.why: expected outcome based on a plan → should

items.sentence: You ___ be joking — there's no way the trip was cancelled.
items.why: strong deduction about the present → must

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct modal form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: Sofia's bag is still on her desk, so she ___ (not/leave) the building yet.
The lights in the gym are on; the team ___ (train) right now.
Nadia looks confused by the question, so she ___ (not/read) the instructions carefully.
I'm not certain, but Liam ___ (forget) about the meeting — he's usually so reliable.
The email was sent an hour ago, so it ___ (arrive) in your inbox by now.
There's no answer at the door; they ___ (go) out for the afternoon.
He's still wearing his football kit, so he ___ (play) a match earlier.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: I'm almost certain Nadia forgot about the deadline.
It's impossible that they saw the message before the trip.
Perhaps Liam is still waiting outside the library.
I'm sure it wasn't Mateo who broke the window.
It's likely that the results are already on the website.

summary: Choose the modal by how certain the evidence makes you feel, from can't (impossible) to must (almost certain).
For now: modal + infinitive — She must be at home.
For the past: modal + have + past participle — She must have gone home.
Mustn't means prohibition, never a negative deduction — use can't for that.
An action in progress at that moment needs the continuous form: must have been training.
